items.content_html:
Summary

The max attribute of a <col> element in xl/worksheets/sheetN.xml is read verbatim on open with no check against MaxColumns, and flatCols() then walks Min..Max doing a deepcopy.Copy and append per iteration. Executed: max="300000", only about 18x past the real 16384 limit, cost 46.2 s of CPU and 122 MB on a single SetColWidth call, and the growth is linear in max up to 2^31-1.

Confirmed at ae2113b (HEAD at the time of audit).

Details

col.go:547, flatCols(), with the two loops at :549 and :564:

for i := col.Min; i <= col.Max; i++ {
...
for i := column.Min; i <= column.Max; i++ { ... fc = append(fc, deepcopy.Copy(...)) }

column.Min and column.Max are plain int attributes on xmlWorksheet.go:279-280, bound straight from the file. MaxColumns is 16384 (templates.go:176) and nothing in the parse path compares against it.

The contrast that makes this an oversight rather than a design decision is inside the callers themselves. SetColWidth validates its own column argument through parseColRange, which clamps to MaxColumns. But flatCols iterates ws.Cols.Col, the file-loaded slice, so the caller's validated argument never constrains the loop. The crafted column expands no matter which column the caller touches.

The row axis has the guard this axis is missing: GHSA-h69g-9hx6-f3v4 capped checkSheet's row allocation at TotalRows, and GHSA-q5j5-6p94-4gwc capped streaming Rows.Next. There is no column-axis equivalent.

Public entry points that flatten the existing columns: SetColWidth (col.go:498 into :534), SetColStyle (col.go:431 into :477), SetColVisible (col.go:282 into :313), SetColOutlineLevel (col.go:376 into :407).

PoC

Executed in-package: crafted a real xlsx, rezipped with an injected <cols> block before <sheetData>, opened it with OpenReader, then called SetColWidth.

<cols><col min="1" max="2147483647" width="9"/></cols>

f.SetColWidth("Sheet1", "A", "A", 12)

Measured:

  • max="300000": 46.2 s CPU, 122 MB allocated, ws.Cols.Col grew to 300000 entries, from one call.
  • max="5000000": did not complete in 110 s, killed by the test timeout.

Growth is linear in max. At max=2147483647 that is roughly two billion xlsxCol allocations, which is hundreds of gigabytes and in practice a permanent hang ending in OOM.

Impact

Any service that opens an untrusted spreadsheet and calls a column mutator. The input is a few dozen bytes of XML inside an otherwise ordinary workbook, no authentication is involved beyond whatever gates the upload, and the process is either wedged for minutes or killed by the OOM reaper. Availability only; no read or write primitive here.

Suggested fix

Validate col.Min and col.Max against MinColumns/MaxColumns when parsing the <col> element, or at the top of flatCols, returning ErrColumnNumber for out-of-range values. That mirrors what checkRowNum already does on the row axis.

Why this is not GHSA-h69g-9hx6-f3v4 or GHSA-q5j5-6p94-4gwc

Both of those are row-axis allocation bounds, and both fixes cap at TotalRows. Neither touched <col> parsing or flatCols. This is the same weakness class on the column axis, and it is arguably worse than the two that were fixed, because those had a cap that was bypassed while this one has no cap at all.

References

  • https://github.com/qax-os/excelize/security/advisories/GHSA-fq3v-74gv-27gm
  • https://github.com/qax-os/excelize/pull/2370
  • https://github.com/qax-os/excelize/commit/a54c578af309fa81f448143ed2b7a91192cc58a7
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-107223
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-fq3v-74gv-27gm

Summary

An attacker who can modify the attested workload’s code, memory-backed state, or configuration after the initial attestation — but without necessarily terminating the existing TLS connection — can cause the peer to continue trusting the connection as if the originally attested state were still running.

Details

Once attestation is successfully appraised and connection is established, there is a window of vulnerability from the establishment of connection to the termination of connection where an attacker can modify the state of the workload and platform at runtime on the TLS endpoint acting as the Attester. Workload state includes code, data, and configuration. Other examples of state changes at the workload level include cases where a new device (such as a GPU) is connected, or where a connected device is disconnected, since the connection establishment.

In Cocos AI, there is no mechanism for the peer to know that some state has changed in the Attester after the connection establishment. The vulnerability is particularly concerning for long-lived connections.

In short, this vulnerability was possible because Cocos AI performs attestation only once in the lifetime of the connection (at connection establishment time) and the verifying peer continues to believe that the state is the same as in initial Evidence throughout, whereas it could be stale at some point in time.

This vulnerability for Cocos AI was found and demonstrated by Muhammad Usama Sardar via formal analysis. Formal analysis was performed in the state-of-the-art tool, ProVerif.

Workarounds

The proposed workaround is to allow re-attestation of the workload after periodic or user-defined intervals using post-handshake attestation.

Background and General Technical Details

For background and general (not specific to Cocos AI) technical details on this vulnerability, please see G-RA2: Freshness of Evidence in Sec. 5.1.1 of Identity Crisis in Confidential Computing: Formal Analysis of Attested TLS. Also, see the corresponding formal analysis.

Credits

This vulnerability for Cocos AI was found and responsibly disclosed by Muhammad Usama Sardar (TU Dresden, Germany).

items.content_html:
Summary

gopacket decodes SCTP (IP protocol 132) by walking the chunk chain through per-chunk-type decoder functions (decodeSCTPInit, decodeSCTPShutdown, decodeSCTPError, decodeSCTPSack, in layers/sctp.go). Each of these reads fixed-size header fields and runs count-driven loops without validating the chunk's declared length against the minimums those reads require. A single crafted SCTP segment causes a runtime panic (out-of-bounds slice read, or inverted slice from unsigned length arithmetic) on any decode path that does not install gopacket's per-packet panic recovery (gopacket.DecodeOptions.SkipDecodeRecovery: true); with the default API the same input degrades to a per-packet decode error.

The defect is present in every released version through v1.7.1 and at current master (18c5805). It is the SCTP component named - but not remediated - in CVE-2026-65819 (GHSA-8mcr-459q-5mx2, "Multiple layer decoders panic …", patched per advisory metadata in v1.7.1). The v1.7.1 hardening commit b772f56 ("layers:various: add protocol decoder length checks (#163)") added generic bounds to the chunk dispatcher and decodeSCTPChunk, but left every chunk sub-decoder without a per-type minimum-length check. The advisory's own description lists "SCTP chunk/parameter decoders (sctp.go)" among items "being confirmed; they should be remediated together with the above" - this report demonstrates that, at v1.7.1 and HEAD, that remediation still does not exist.

Patches

Fixed in v1.7.2 by commit 5080443 ("layers/sctp: bound chunk sub-decoders and parameters"). INIT/INIT-ACK, SACK and SHUTDOWN now check their chunk type's minimum length, SACK rejects gap-ack and duplicate-TSN counts the chunk can't hold, and decodeSCTPParameter rejects TLV lengths below 4 or beyond the buffer. Each case returns a decode error instead of panicking. The same commit fixes a panic on valid input, where a final parameter's padding lies outside the chunk length (RFC 9260 3.2). Regression tests: TestDecodeSCTPChunkRegression and TestDecodeSCTPParameterPadding in layers/decode_oob_test.go.

Upgrade with go get github.com/gopacket/gopacket@v1.7.2.

Workarounds

Before v1.7.2, keep panic recovery on: use gopacket.NewPacket without SkipDecodeRecovery, and DecodingLayerParser with IgnorePanic: false. The crafted packet then fails to decode instead of crashing the process.

Vulnerability Details

All line numbers refer to layers/sctp.go at commit 18c5805028329a6a8944f054d8d3f64ebc0f1373 (master, 2026-09-01; v1.7.1-1-g18c5805).

The shared entry point already present in v1.7.1 validates only that a chunk is present and that its declared length is ≥ 4 and covered by real bytes:

// sctp.go:129
func decodeSCTPChunk(data []byte) (SCTPChunk, error) {
    if len(data) < 4 { ... }
    length := binary.BigEndian.Uint16(data[2:4])
    if length < 4 { ... }
    actual := roundUpToNearest4(int(length))
    ct := SCTPChunkType(data[0])
    if ct == SCTPChunkTypeData && length < 16 { ... }   // only DATA gets a 16-byte minimum
    if len(data) < actual { ... }
    ...

The Data-chunk minimum of 16 bytes is never applied to the other chunk types, and none of the sub-decoders re-check before indexing. Four independent panic paths result (each reproduced at HEAD):

Defect 1 - INIT / INIT-ACK chunks (decodeSCTPInit, sctp.go:423): reads data[4:8], data[8:12] (line 431), data[12:14], data[14:16], data[16:20] (line 434), then slices paramData := data[20:sc.ActualLength] (line 436).

  • Declared length 8–11, actual 8–12 -> data[8:12] reads past the chunk: panic: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [:12] with capacity 8
  • Declared length 15, actual 16 -> data[16:20] past the chunk: panic: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [:20] with capacity 16
  • Declared length ≤ 19 -> the data[20:ActualLength] slice is inverted (panic) or the subsequent parameter loop runs on attacker data without the decodeSCTPParameter length check (Defect 3).

Defect 2 - SHUTDOWN chunks (decodeSCTPShutdown, sctp.go:670): reads binary.BigEndian.Uint32(data[4:8]) (line 677) on a chunk whose declared length is only validated as ≥ 4: panic: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [:8] with capacity 4 (4-byte chunk).

Defect 3 - ERROR (and HEARTBEAT/INIT) parameter decoder (decodeSCTPParameter, sctp.go:193): the crafted Length field is used to slice with no bound against the parameter buffer:

// sctp.go:193
func decodeSCTPParameter(data []byte) SCTPParameter {
    length := binary.BigEndian.Uint16(data[2:4])
    return SCTPParameter{
        ...
        Value:        data[4:length],   // line 198: no check length >= 4 or length <= len(data)
        ActualLength: roundUpToNearest4(int(length)),
    }
}
  • length < 4 -> inverted slice: panic: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [4:0] (reached from decodeSCTPError line 632 paramData := data[4:sc.Length], and from the INIT (438) / HEARTBEAT (578) parameter loops).
  • length > len(data) -> slice-bounds-check panic (Go's slice bounds check panics; the read never silently over-reads).

Defect 4 - SACK chunk count loops (decodeSCTPSack, sctp.go:484): NumGapACKs / NumDuplicateTSNs (attacker-controlled uint16 fields) drive loops that slice the remaining bytes with no bound:

// sctp.go:512
bytesRemaining := data[16:]
for i := 0; i < int(sc.NumGapACKs); i++ {                       // line 513
    sc.GapACKs = append(sc.GapACKs, binary.BigEndian.Uint16(bytesRemaining[:2]))  // line 514
    bytesRemaining = bytesRemaining[2:]
}
for i := 0; i < int(sc.NumDuplicateTSNs); i++ {                 // line 517
    sc.DuplicateTSNs = append(sc.DuplicateTSNs, binary.BigEndian.Uint32(bytesRemaining[:4]))  // line 518
    bytesRemaining = bytesRemaining[4:]
}

A 16-byte SACK chunk declaring NumGapACKs = 1 with no following bytes: panic: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [:2] with capacity 0

Note this is not the sFlow/Diameter "unbounded allocation" family already covered by CVE-2026-54332/CVE-2026-54345; the SACK make() capacities are already capped against ActualLength (lines 505–510) - the loop iteration counts are not, so the panic is an out-of-bounds read, not an allocation.

History / version range. decodeSCTPInit and the chunk sub-decoders were introduced in commit 2fca351 (original full-featured SCTP implementation; at the time the file was named layer_sctp.go - the current sctp.go path dates from the rename in dea6b39). The sinks are present in every release from v1.0.0 through v1.7.1 and at HEAD (also confirmed at v1.6.0). b772f56 (2026-07-08, included in v1.7.1) touched layers/sctp.go but only hardened the dispatcher (decodeWithSCTPChunkTypePrefix) and the generic decodeSCTPChunk/decodeSCTPDataChunk bounds; the four sub-decoder paths above are unchanged by it. The v1.7.1 regression-test commit 2220269 covers the advisory's other decoders, not SCTP chunk sub-decoders. Affected range is therefore every gopacket version: <= 1.7.1, plus current master 18c5805. (Maintainer update: fixed in v1.7.2, commit 5080443; see Patches.)

Relationship to the published advisory (dedup context). CVE-2026-65819 / GHSA-8mcr-459q-5mx2 (published 2026-07-27) declares vulnerable_version_range: <= 1.7.0 / patched_versions: 1.7.1. Its description explicitly names "SCTP chunk/parameter decoders (sctp.go)" among decoder families "(on the recovering path only) … being confirmed; they should be remediated together with the above". Because the advisory metadata tells consumers that upgrading to 1.7.1 remediates the advisory, and this SCTP component was not actually fixed, the practical status of this finding is incomplete remediation of a published advisory: consumers of the 1.7.1 "patched" version remain exposed to the SCTP panic path. The finding is reported here so the maintainers can either complete the SCTP fix under the existing advisory or track it separately.

Impact

An unauthenticated remote attacker can crash a gopacket-based decoder with a single crafted SCTP segment (IP protocol 132). A 54-byte Ethernet frame (Ethernet -> IPv4 -> SCTP with an 8-byte INIT chunk) is enough (see Reproduction Steps). Panic escapes for consumers that disable gopacket's built-in recovery:

  • gopacket.NewPacket(data, layerType, DecodeOptions{SkipDecodeRecovery: true}) - panic propagates to the caller, terminating the process if uncaught.
  • Direct use of the registered SCTP decode chain without recovery.

Two gopacket entry points install recovery by default and are therefore NOT crash surfaces for this bug: gopacket.NewPacket with default options (deferred recover wraps the whole decode chain, converting the panic into a per-packet error, demonstrated in case B below), and DecodingLayerParser.DecodeLayers when IgnorePanic is false (parser.go:306 - if !l.IgnorePanic { defer panicToError(&err) }); in both cases the packet simply fails to decode. Panic escape - and process crash - requires the non-recovering settings above. This mirrors exactly the reachability of the sibling advisories in the same family (GHSA-6h9g MPTCP, GHSA-8mcr): CVE-2026-65819 itself is scored with the same AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N vector while noting (per the GHSA advisory text) ~5.3 (Medium) for recovering-path-only consumers; the reporter scored the non-recovering consumer set at 7.5, which is the configuration used by high-throughput packet-analysis engines that set SkipDecodeRecovery to detect decode failures themselves.

The default API (gopacket.NewPacket(..., gopacket.Default)) installs defer recover and converts the panic into a per-packet decode error, so crash exposure is limited to non-recovering consumers (packet-analysis engines, IDS/NDR pipelines, capture-processing tools that set SkipDecodeRecovery or call decoders directly - the same consumer set described in the CVE-2026-65819 and CVE-2026-54332/54345 advisories).

Impact is availability only: no memory disclosure, no code execution, no allocation amplification. Severity: CVSS 3.1 5.9 Medium - CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H (reporter proposed 7.5 with AC:L; maintainers set AC:H because a crash needs the consumer to disable panic recovery), primary CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read), secondaries CWE-129 (improper validation of array index for the inverted slices).

Per-metric justification (primary vector):

  • Attack Vector (AV): Network - a single crafted SCTP segment (IP protocol 132) delivered over the wire triggers the panic path; no local access needed.
  • Attack Complexity (AC): High - the input is trivial (a 54-byte frame with an 8-byte INIT chunk), but a crash depends on a condition outside the attacker's control: the target must have disabled gopacket's panic recovery. Default configurations only produce a decode error.
  • Privileges Required (PR): None - the decoding library processes untrusted captured/live packets with no authentication.
  • User Interaction (UI): None - no victim action; the crash occurs during automated decode.
  • Scope (S): Unchanged - the impacted security authority is the decoder's own process (the caller's application).
  • Confidentiality (C): None - no data disclosure.
  • Integrity (I): None - no data modification.
  • Availability (A): High - non-recovering consumer process terminates (panic); the ~5.3 recovering-path-only alternative is disclosed above.

Reproduction Steps

Environment: Go 1.25 toolchain (module requires go 1.25.0), github.com/gopacket/gopacket at HEAD 18c5805028329a6a8944f054d8d3f64ebc0f1373 (v1.7.1 + 1 commit). The same output is produced at tag v1.7.1.

// repro_sctp.go - single static input, one deterministic observable (decode panic)
package main

import (
    "fmt"

    "github.com/gopacket/gopacket"
    "github.com/gopacket/gopacket/layers"
)

func main() {
    // One 54-byte frame: Ethernet -> IPv4(proto 132) -> SCTP -> INIT chunk (declared length 8)
    frame := []byte{
        // Ethernet
        0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0x00, 0x11, 0x22, 0x33, 0x44, 0x55, 0x08, 0x00,
        // IPv4, protocol 132 (SCTP), total length 40
        0x45, 0x00, 0x00, 0x28, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x84, 0x00, 0x84,
        0x0a, 0x00, 0x00, 0x01, 0x0a, 0x00, 0x00, 0x02,
        // SCTP common header (12 bytes)
        0x11, 0x11, 0x22, 0x22, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00,
        // INIT chunk: type=1, flags=0, length=8 (declared), body 4 bytes
        0x01, 0x00, 0x00, 0x08, 0xaa, 0xbb, 0xcc, 0xdd,
    }
    // same bytes as hex:
    // ffffffffffff00112233445508004500002800000000008400840a0000010a000002
    // 1111222200000000000000000100000008aabbccdd

    // A) Non-recovering decode (SkipDecodeRecovery: true) -> panic escapes
    func() {
        defer func() {
            if r := recover(); r != nil {
                fmt.Printf("A) SkipDecodeRecovery=true  -> PANIC: %v\n", r)
            }
        }()
        p := gopacket.NewPacket(frame, layers.LayerTypeEthernet,
            gopacket.DecodeOptions{Lazy: false, SkipDecodeRecovery: true})
        _ = p.Dump()
        fmt.Println("A) no panic (unexpected)")
    }()

    // B) Default (recovering) API -> per-packet error, process survives
    p := gopacket.NewPacket(frame, layers.LayerTypeEthernet, gopacket.Default)
    fmt.Printf("B) Default (recovering)    -> err=%v  layers=%d\n", p.ErrorLayer(), len(p.Layers()))
}

Build and run (module file go.mod):

module repro

go 1.25.0

require github.com/gopacket/gopacket v1.7.1

replace github.com/gopacket/gopacket => /path/to/clone/of/gopacket/gopacket  # at 18c5805 (or tag v1.7.1)

$ go build -o repro_sctp repro_sctp.go
$ ./repro_sctp
A) SkipDecodeRecovery=true  -> PANIC: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [:12] with capacity 8
B) Default (recovering)    -> err=Packet decoding error: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [:12] with capacity 8  layers=4

Observed stack (case A): layers.decodeSCTPInit at layers/sctp.go:431 <- SCTPChunkType.Decode <- decodeWithSCTPChunkTypePrefix (sctp.go:57) <- decodeSCTP (sctp.go:38) <- NewPacket.

Additional one-input repros for the other three defect classes (same harness shape, decode root LayerTypeSCTP with SkipDecodeRecovery: true):

Input Panic (observed) Sink
INIT-ACK chunk type 2, declared length 8 slice bounds out of range [:12] with capacity 8 sctp.go:431
INIT chunk declared length 15, 12-byte body slice bounds out of range [:20] with capacity 16 sctp.go:434
SACK chunk type 3, length 16, NumGapACKs=1, NumDuplicateTSNs=1, no trailing bytes slice bounds out of range [:2] with capacity 0 sctp.go:514
SHUTDOWN chunk type 7, declared length 4 slice bounds out of range [:8] with capacity 4 sctp.go:677
ERROR chunk type 9, length 8, 4-byte "parameter" with Length field 0 slice bounds out of range [4:0] sctp.go:198

Recommendations

Complete the v1.7.1 remediation by validating each chunk subtype's declared length against the fixed-size fields and loops that consume it, immediately after decodeSCTPChunk succeeds in each sub-decoder. Minimal correct changes in layers/sctp.go:

  1. decodeSCTPInit: require sc.ActualLength >= 20 before reading data[4:20] (return a decode error otherwise), then bound the parameter loop: paramData := data[20:sc.ActualLength] is safe once the chunk length is ≥ 20 and decodeSCTPParameter is hardened (below).
  2. decodeSCTPShutdown: require sc.ActualLength >= 8.
  3. decodeSCTPSack: require sc.ActualLength >= 16, and cap the loops - iterate min(NumGapACKs, remaining/2) and min(NumDuplicateTSNs, remaining/4), returning an error (or silently stopping with SetTruncated) when a count exceeds the bytes available.
  4. decodeSCTPParameter (shared by INIT/HEARTBEAT/ERROR): reject length < 4 and length > len(data) before the data[4:length] slice, mirroring the bound style already used for TCP options (tcp.go default branch) - this closes Defect 3 at its root regardless of which loop calls it.

Optionally add regression tests in the style of 2220269 covering short INIT/SHUTDOWN/SACK/ERROR chunks.

Resources

  • Source at pin: layers/sctp.go @ https://github.com/gopacket/gopacket/blob/18c5805028329a6a8944f054d8d3f64ebc0f1373/layers/sctp.go (lines 129–136 dispatcher/chunk guard, 193–202 decodeSCTPParameter, 423–442 decodeSCTPInit, 484–521 decodeSCTPSack, 670–678 decodeSCTPShutdown, 623–636 decodeSCTPError)
  • Fix commit that missed the sub-decoders: https://github.com/gopacket/gopacket/commit/b772f566a3ecc53c099bdd44eab4718088c4e866 (PR #163, "layers:various: add protocol decoder length checks")
  • Regression-test commit: https://github.com/gopacket/gopacket/commit/2220269 (v1.7.1, "test(layers): add regression tests for the decoder panic advisories")
  • Advisory that names the unfixed SCTP component: https://github.com/gopacket/gopacket/security/advisories/GHSA-8mcr-459q-5mx2 (CVE-2026-65819, "Multiple layer decoders panic on crafted packets …, including (on the recovering path only) … SCTP chunk/parameter decoders (sctp.go)"); NVD: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-65819
  • Sibling advisory with identical reachability framing (High 7.5): https://github.com/gopacket/gopacket/security/advisories/GHSA-6h9g-cjv3-pg2c (TCP MPTCP option decoder)
  • Introduced in: https://github.com/gopacket/gopacket/commit/2fca351 (original SCTP implementation)

Summary

The traversal fix for CVE-2026-33344 was implemented as HTTP middleware installed only in the chi handler chain, but the MCP service calls the same API method in process, so arbitrary YAML file read is reachable again through the MCP tool surface with a viewer-role key. Read-only, limited to .yaml/.yml targets. Confirmed at HEAD f6c039f (post v2.10.7).

The defect

The fix for CVE-2026-33344 is a reflection-based HTTP middleware (internal/frontend/.../api.go, roughly lines 553-597) that inspects a request field named FileName and rejects anything that is not a plain name. It is installed in exactly one place: the chi strict-handler chain (api.go around line 419).

The MCP service does not go through that chain. internal/service/mcp/server.go calls the API method directly as an in-process Go call:

func (svc *Service) getDAGSpec(ctx context.Context, name string) (map[string]any, error) {   // line 307
    resp, err := svc.api.GetDAGSpec(ctx, daguapi.GetDAGSpecRequestObject{
        FileName: daguapi.DAGFileName(name),                                                 // line 309
    })

No HTTP request is constructed, so no middleware executes, and the underlying resolver is still uncontained:

func (store *Storage) locateDAG(nameOrPath string) (string, error) {                 // line 1041
    if strings.Contains(nameOrPath, string(filepath.Separator)) {                    // line 1042
        foundPath, err := findDAGFile(nameOrPath)
        if err == nil {
            return foundPath, nil                                                    // line 1045, no containment check
        }
    }

An absolute path contains a separator, so it takes the first branch and is returned as-is, with no check that it falls under store.baseDir or any entry in store.searchPaths.

Verification

Verified end to end using the project's own conformance/mcptest harness against a real running HTTP server, not by source reading:

dagu_read {"target":"dag_spec","name":"/abs/outside/secret.yaml"}
-> HTTP 200, full file contents returned in data.spec

This also succeeded with a viewer-role API key on an auth-enabled server (auth.mode: builtin), so it is not admin-only. Control test that makes this a residual: the equivalent REST request is correctly blocked (400, "name must only contain alphanumeric characters..."). The HTTP lane is fixed; the MCP lane is not.

Bounded impact: read only (dagu_change and dagu_execute are both blocked by spec-level name validation; I tested both); only .yaml/.yml targets. Secondary: GetDAGSpec skips the requireWorkspaceVisible check its sibling handlers run, so this also crosses workspace isolation.

Suggested fix

Move the containment check out of HTTP middleware and into locateDAG itself, rejecting any resolved path that does not fall under baseDir or a configured search path. A middleware that runs on only one of two transports into the same API cannot hold the boundary; the resolver is the correct chokepoint since both transports converge there. Separately, add requireWorkspaceVisible to GetDAGSpec to match its siblings.

Tooling

AI assistance was used while investigating. The traversal was reproduced against a real running server through the project's own MCP conformance harness, including with a viewer-role API key, and the REST control test confirms the HTTP lane is blocked. Confirmed in the uncontained locateDAG branch and the direct in-process GetDAGSpec call at HEAD.

Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines frontend reflected untrusted pod names and namespaces into HTML error responses from the pod-information and pod-events routes. An attacker could craft a link that causes JavaScript to execute in the frontend's origin when a user follows it and reaches an affected error response.

Affected routes include /pipeline/k8s/pod and /pipeline/k8s/pod/events (the deployment's configured base path may differ).

Impact and prerequisites

Successful exploitation requires a victim to open an attacker-supplied link and reach the vulnerable response. JavaScript execution may expose information accessible to the victim's browser or perform actions in the application's origin.

The attacker does not need an account merely to construct and deliver the link. The victim must satisfy the deployment's authentication and route-access requirements. Cookie theft depends on cookie attributes and deployment protections; it is not guaranteed. The submitted evidence does not establish an availability impact or server-side code execution.

Technical details

The pod handlers pass podname and podnamespace query values to getPod and listPodEvents in frontend/server/k8s-helper.ts. Before remediation, failure messages incorporated those values, along with backend error details, and were returned as HTML-capable string responses.

Kubernetes rejecting an invalid resource name did not prevent the issue: the rejected name could still be included in the frontend's error response.

PR #12295 changed the error construction to validate pod names and namespaces with isAllowedResourceName. Invalid values produce a constant error message instead of reflecting the supplied value, and backend error details are no longer included in these responses. The change includes invalid-resource-name tests.

Affected versions and remediation

Affected product: the Kubeflow Pipelines frontend server, identified as ghcr.io/kubeflow/kfp-frontend. Historical releases may use earlier image registry names.

Upgrade to KFP 2.15.0 or later.

The fix merged on October 10, 2025, in commit fedc25e3f7251933d4a37b964bc3e8176beea28e. It is first present in the 2.15.0 release, published November 25, 2025.

The affected range is recorded as < 2.15.0. The original introduction version and separate maintenance-branch backports have not been established. These are KFP component versions, not Kubeflow platform or Python SDK versions.

Distinction from existing artifact XSS

CVE-2023-6571, tracked in the repository as GHSA-j9xw-rrjg-2p9r, documents reflection of the artifact source parameter in an unknown-storage-source error.

This report concerns different handlers and error construction: pod information and pod events. The artifact-source fix in PR #9844, released in 2.0.2, did not repair these pod responses. They required the later change in #12295.

This independently fixable pod-route defect is tracked as CVE-2026-88986. It does not broaden CVE-2023-6571 or absorb artifact-content rendering and other XSS reports.

Attribution

@pwny0 submitted this report on September 23, 2023, and retains the reporter credit.

@JerT33 authored the remediation in PR #12295. Fix attribution is separate from vulnerability-report attribution.

Summary

Kubeflow Pipelines API server does not sufficiently validate SQL identifier fields decoded from the page_token pagination parameter. Client-controlled fields can reach SQL query construction, allowing SQL injection through list APIs.

This advisory consolidates the original pipeline-listing report and the later run-listing report in GHSA-mhpc-2x8q-2vp9. Their contributions and chronology are distinguished below.

Impact and prerequisites

An attacker able to invoke an affected list API may read data accessible to the API server's database account, including data belonging to other namespaces. The original report demonstrated database read access through an authenticated Kubeflow deployment.

Authentication and authorization requirements depend on deployment configuration. In multi-user deployments, the attacker must pass the applicable endpoint authorization checks. A single-user deployment that exposes the API without an authentication layer may be reachable without credentials.

The submitted evidence establishes a confidentiality issue. Database modification was not demonstrated; this advisory does not claim arbitrary database writes.

Technical details

Pagination tokens are base64-encoded JSON, not trusted server-side state. Before the fix, token deserialization accepted structural fields such as key and sort identifiers without sufficient validation before SQL construction.

The reports describe complementary paths through this defect:

  • Pipeline listing: the original report demonstrated injection through KeyFieldName.
  • Run listing: the later report documented SortByFieldName reaching query construction in both the v1beta1 and v2beta1 APIs, including metric joins, selected column aliases, ordering, and column propagation through resource-reference and task joins.

These paths share the unvalidated pagination-token boundary. Review of the later report and its discussion identified no reported path left unresolved by the merged fix.

Remediation

Upgrade the Kubeflow Pipelines API server to 2.17.0 or later.

PR #13127, included in 2.17.0, validates token identifiers and filter keys before query construction. It also separates user-facing metric names from SQL identifiers, uses a fixed metric-column alias, and parameterizes the metric-name join condition.

The PR additionally addresses first-page metric sorting without a pagination token. That additional protection is part of the remediation; the duplicate determination here concerns the page-token claims actually submitted in the two reports, not merely their inclusion in the same PR.

The original report identified its deployment as Kubeflow 1.7, which should not be interpreted as a verified Kubeflow Pipelines component-version boundary. The later report identified KFP 2.16.0. These are reported affected environments, not an established introduction version.

Attribution and report history

  • @phisch1991 and @k0rti: credited reporters of the original pipeline-listing SQL injection submitted on December 13, 2023.
  • BugBunny.ai (@bugbunny-research): submitted the later report on April 1, 2026, documenting the run-listing and metric-query paths in GHSA-mhpc-2x8q-2vp9. This acknowledges that specific contribution without implying authorship of the 2023 report.
  • Cyber Nagle: authored the merged remediation in PR #13127.

GHSA-mhpc-2x8q-2vp9 is consolidated here for vulnerability tracking. Its submission and reporter credit remain preserved on that advisory; closure as a duplicate does not characterize the report as invalid.

Summary

In multi-user mode, the Kubeflow Pipelines API server skipped authorization checks for shared/global pipelines with an empty namespace. This exception applied to write and delete operations as well as reads, allowing an authenticated user to modify or delete shared pipelines without the required Kubernetes RBAC permissions.

Impact

Unauthorized modification compromises the integrity of shared pipeline definitions and versions. Unauthorized deletion can make shared pipelines unavailable.

Execution of a modified pipeline can cause attacker-controlled workload behavior, but this is a conditional downstream consequence requiring the modified pipeline to be executed. Modification alone does not demonstrate immediate worker code execution.

Reading shared pipelines is intentionally permitted and remains permitted after the fix. Consequently, access to shared pipeline configuration does not establish an additional confidentiality impact from this write-authorization defect. The confidentiality metric is None; the integrity and availability metrics reflect unauthorized modification and deletion of shared pipelines.

The affected authorization boundary is shared pipelines in multi-user deployments. Single-user deployments intentionally bypass these multi-user authorization checks.

Patches

Fixed by kubeflow/pipelines#13288, with the fix included in 2.16.1.

Read-only operations on shared pipelines remain allowed. For write and delete operations, the API server checks Kubernetes RBAC permissions against the KFP system namespace, because shared pipelines have no namespace of their own.

Scope of this fix

The 2.16.1 fix addresses the shared-pipeline authorization paths described above. It does not fix every shared-pipeline write path: the separate shared-pipeline upload authorization defect is tracked in GHSA-rjr3-43j3-4q8g / CVE-2026-77596. Consult that advisory for its affected versions and remediation; 2.16.1 must not be interpreted as fixing that separate upload defect.

Workarounds

Until upgrading, restrict access to the Pipelines API to trusted users through deployment-level access controls. Namespace RBAC alone does not correct the affected shared-pipeline authorization path.

Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines API server fetched caller-supplied pipeline package URLs without restricting the destination. A caller authorized to create a pipeline or pipeline version could cause requests to originate from the API server's network position, including to internal services that the caller could not otherwise reach.

Impact

The reported evidence demonstrates blind server-side request forgery and a limited status-code oracle. The fetched response is processed as a pipeline package; the report does not demonstrate arbitrary response-body disclosure or credential theft. A request to a cloud metadata endpoint returned HTTP 403, which does not establish access to metadata contents or tokens.

The confidentiality metric is Low to reflect the limited information obtainable through the status-code oracle. High confidentiality impact and integrity or availability impact are not established by the submitted evidence. Impact depends on the API server's network reachability and the deployment's trust boundaries.

Patches

Fixed by kubeflow/pipelines#12750, first released in 2.17.0. The fix validates URL schemes, ports, allowed domains, and resolved IP addresses; validates redirects; and enforces IP restrictions at connection time. The HTTP client also applies timeouts and disables environment proxy use so connections pass through the validated dialer.

Operators should keep pipeline URL validation enabled and limit additional allowed domains to trusted pipeline sources.

Workarounds

Until upgrading, restrict API-server egress to required destinations through deployment-specific network controls. Account for required Kubernetes and storage connectivity when applying these restrictions.

Related reports

This is the canonical advisory for the API-server pipeline URL SSRF family. GHSA-wg4h-pp3x-hxhv is tracked as a duplicate submission. Each submission retains its own reporter attribution; this cross-link does not transfer authorship.

Earlier related submission

@pwny0's GHSA-fxx8-rx8w-p9v7, submitted September 23, 2023, included an earlier report of external interaction through the API-server pipeline-package URL path. That portion is consolidated here; its namespace-based frontend SSRF is tracked separately under GHSA-895m-3hxm-h4mg / CVE-2023-6570.

This acknowledges the earlier pipeline-URL submission without attributing fxx8's frontend response-disclosure or cookie-forwarding evidence to the API-server path. @pwny0 retains reporter credit on fxx8; @gasbugs retains reporter credit for this submission. items.content_html:
Summary

The legacy Kubeflow Pipelines V1/raw-Argo execution cache does not separate cached results by Kubernetes namespace. In multi-user deployments where tenants share the cache service, a tenant can receive another tenant's cached outputs or seed outputs that are subsequently substituted into another tenant's step.

This affects the Argo-template cache mutating webhook and its cache-server storage path. Standard KFP V2 component pods bypass this webhook cache; the separate V2 cache implementation is outside this advisory's scope.

Affected deployments and impact

The issue requires multiple tenant namespaces sharing the legacy cache service, cache-enabled V1/raw-Argo steps, and cache entries that satisfy the configured staleness policy. The standard multi-user configuration watches pods across namespaces.

A tenant able to submit a step with the same cache-relevant template fields as another tenant's step can:

  • Read cached step outputs originally produced in another namespace.
  • Populate the shared cache before another tenant's matching step runs, causing that step to report the cached outputs instead of executing its intended containers.

Matching refers to the selected template fields used by the cache key, not merely an identical container image. This is an application-level cache-key collision caused by missing tenant scope, not a cryptographic SHA-256 collision. The finding establishes cross-namespace confidentiality and integrity impact; it does not establish arbitrary code execution.

CVSS rationale

Medium — CVSS 3.1: 5.4

CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N

  • AV:N / PR:L / UI:N: a tenant with ordinary workload-submission privileges can exercise the shared cache through network-accessible APIs. Reading an existing cached result or poisoning a subsequent automated execution requires no additional victim interaction.
  • AC:L: known or shared templates can produce the same cache key deterministically. Cache-enabled execution and matching template fields describe the affected configuration; they do not establish an unavoidable narrow race or secret prerequisite.
  • S:U: the established impact is disclosure or substitution of output data managed by the same cache service. Crossing tenant namespaces alone does not establish a change in security authority; execution under a separate victim authority has not been established here.
  • C:L / I:L / A:N: the confirmed impact is selective cached-output disclosure and substitution. Arbitrary code execution, complete workload compromise, and a service-availability impact are not established.

Root cause

The vulnerable implementation hashes selected Argo template fields without a namespace. Cache lookups and duplicate checks use the key alone, and stored rows have no namespace ownership field. On a hit, the admission handler restores cached outputs and substitutes a dummy container for the step's containers.

The completion watcher also trusts the mutable pipelines.kubeflow.org/execution_cache_key annotation when publishing outputs. Adding a namespace to the hash alone is therefore insufficient: a tenant able to patch its own pod could supply another namespace's deterministic key. Namespace ownership must be enforced independently on cache writes and reads.

Relevant implementation files are backend/src/cache/server/mutation.go, backend/src/cache/server/watcher.go, backend/src/cache/storage/execution_cache_store.go, and backend/src/cache/model/execution_cache.go.

Fix status

The source fix merged on September 10, 2026 in PR #14359, commit 620d0cc89ae0d042a484a003f8ffe6e9a55d347e.

The merged fix:

  • Derives namespaced keys from the API server's admission request namespace and selected template fields.
  • Recomputes completed pods' keys from their observed namespace and ARGO_TEMPLATE, rejecting mismatched or malformed identities rather than trusting the annotation.
  • Stores the observed namespace separately and scopes normal reads and duplicate detection by namespace and key.
  • Adds a namespace column and composite index, leaving historical rows unowned and excluded from normal lookups.
  • Rejects structurally malformed template objects without panicking.

The first fixed release is 2.18.0. Releases through 2.17.3 remain affected; the affected-version upper bound is <= 2.17.3 and the patched version is 2.18.0.

Upgrade requirements and legacy fallback

The standard cache-server Deployment supports a normal rolling upgrade from 2.17.2. Apply the upgraded manifests without manually stopping old replicas or pausing submissions. Namespace isolation is fully enforced only after all old cache-server processes, including terminating pods, have exited and every new replica uses enforce. Custom installations sharing the cache database must upgrade every writer. Mixed-version operation does not yet provide the full isolation guarantee.

Expect reduced cache reuse and increased step execution/resource use as tasks next run; there is no startup cache rebuild. Do not infer or backfill namespace ownership for historical rows. Pre-upgrade pods carrying old-format keys do not seed the new namespaced cache. Completing the upgrade does not undo previously disclosed data or reused poisoned outputs. Do not roll back to the vulnerable implementation to recover cache hits.

PR #14427 merged into release-2.18 on October 5, 2026 and standardizes the compatibility setting as KFP_SECURITY_LEGACY_CACHE_MODE=enforce|audit on the cache-server Deployment. This supersedes the original fix's ALLOW_LEGACY_CACHE_FALLBACK interface. Unset, empty, or enforce keeps full namespace isolation; invalid values prevent startup.

Explicit audit permits a genuine namespaced cache miss to reuse a historical template-only entry whose stored namespace is empty. That entry may contain another tenant's outputs, including poisoned outputs: audit accepts residual cross-tenant confidentiality and integrity risk, and is not full remediation. Scoped entries take precedence, known foreign namespaces remain excluded, and a database error does not enable legacy fallback. Legacy hits are not promoted or backfilled into namespaced rows.

The server emits a startup warning and scoped security_audit events for legacy reuse without logging cached outputs or credentials. Keep replicas configured consistently, persist the mode in deployment configuration, and return to enforce after migration. Native V2 caching is outside this control and this advisory.

See the released cache-server guide for rollout completion checks and audit-to-enforce migration. This fix does not establish an integrity boundary between users who can modify workloads within the same namespace.

Mitigation until the fixed release is deployed

Disable legacy cache reuse for affected workloads, or ensure mutually untrusted namespaces do not share the legacy cache service and storage. Restricting the webhook's namespace selector or watcher scope alone is insufficient if mutually untrusted tenants still share cached entries.

Validation

Source review identified the shared key, unscoped storage, and mutable-annotation write path. The public fix includes regressions exercising admission and completion handling, forged foreign-namespace keys, normal same-namespace reuse, malformed templates, legacy-row exclusion, and optional fallback behavior.

During development, the cache test suite and lint passed; populated and repeatable schema migration and scoped storage behavior were verified on SQLite, MySQL 8.4, and PostgreSQL 16. Negative controls removing the watcher identity check or storage namespace filter failed their corresponding regressions. These tests use fake Kubernetes clients; they are not a claim of a live multi-tenant Kubernetes exploit reproduction.

Private patch disposition

The earlier private PR #1 is closed as superseded by public PR #14359 and the released follow-ups described above. The private branch and review history are retained; this closure does not dismiss the report or change reporter credit. The advisory remains a draft pending the publication review.

items.content_html:
Summary

croc is an end-to-end encrypted peer-to-peer file transfer tool. On the receiving side, the confirmation that normally protects an existing file from being overwritten or resumed is skipped whenever the received file's name starts with croc-stdin-, regardless of whether the incoming transfer is actually a text transfer. A sender can therefore name a file croc-stdin-<existing-name> and silently overwrite, truncate, or replace an existing file of that name in the receiver's working directory - including removing the existing file and substituting a symlink - without the Overwrite? prompt that the standard path requires. The exemption was introduced to keep croc's internal text-transfer artifacts from triggering prompts, but it is keyed on the filename prefix rather than on the transfer type, so any ordinary file transfer can claim the exemption.

Vulnerability Details

Affected code at commit b6f27da9401f2c3647c1adb6b77a46bb8c0923d2 (HEAD, v11.5.1+1):

The receive-side file-readiness loop in src/croc/croc.go decides whether to prompt before overwriting or resuming an existing destination file. The decision is made around line 3413:

isStdinName := strings.HasPrefix(path.Base(fileInfo.Name), "croc-stdin-")
...
if destinationExists && !c.Options.Overwrite && !c.Options.Rename && !isStdinName {
    resumable := fileInfo.Size > 0 && fileInfo.Symlink == "" && recipientFileInfo.Mode().IsRegular()
    overwrite, promptErr := askReceiveOverwrite(c.clientContext(), fileInfo, resumable)
    if promptErr != nil {
        return promptErr
    }
    if !overwrite {
        continue
    }
}

isStdinName is derived purely from the received file's basename. The prompt is suppressed for any such name, even when c.Options.SendingText is false and the transfer is an ordinary file transfer whose name the sender chose.

When the prompt is skipped and the transfer declares fileInfo.Size == 0 or a symlink (fileInfo.Symlink != ""), the loop calls createEmptyFileAndFinish() (src/croc/croc.go:3245), which - before creating the new entry - removes any existing file at the destination:

if fileInfo.Symlink != "" {
    if err = validateReceiveSymlinkTarget(fileInfo.FolderRemote, fileInfo.Symlink); err != nil {
        return
    }
    log.Debug("creating symlink")
    // remove symlink if it exists
    if _, errExists := root.Lstat(pathToFile); errExists == nil {
        if err = root.Remove(pathToFile); err != nil {
            return err
        }
    }
    err = root.Symlink(fileInfo.Symlink, pathToFile)
    ...
}

For a normal (non-croc-stdin-) name, the overwrite prompt runs first, so the remove/replace step only happens with the user's explicit y. For a croc-stdin- name the entire prompt is bypassed: an existing croc-stdin-* file is deleted and replaced with the attacker's symlink (or, for Size == 0, truncated to an empty file) with no confirmation.

For a non-empty regular-file transfer with a croc-stdin- name, the same missing prompt lets the receive path proceed through recipientInitializeFile() (src/croc/croc.go:3109; the os.O_RDWR open is at 3136-3138): the existing file is opened O_RDWR (no O_EXCL), truncated to the sender-declared size when the sizes differ, and the sender's chunks are written at the declared offsets - a silent overwrite of the existing file's content.

Why the check is missing: the exemption was added deliberately so that croc's own croc-stdin-* text artifacts (created by os.CreateTemp(".", "croc-stdin-") for croc send --text / piped stdin) do not trigger an overwrite question every time. History: commit b687778d "bug fix: doesn't ask overwrite text Fixes #384" (2021-04-29) introduced the prefix-based skip, keyed on the filename and not on the transfer's SendingText flag. The branch that handles Size == 0 || Symlink != "" via createEmptyFileAndFinish() predates that (6386e4a8, 2019) and at the time ran unconditionally for every received name; the refactor 615af377 "fix: gate overwrites and receive hash algorithms" (2026-08-29, first released in v11.3.6) moved it below the overwrite-prompt gate, so after v11.3.6 the empty-file/symlink replacement reaches the remove-and-replace step without user confirmation only through the croc-stdin- exemption. The refactor extracted the prefix test into isStdinName and kept it filename-only, dropping the explicit !c.Options.SendingText conjunct that the pre-refactor prompt conditions still carried (615af377~1); the original intent was to suppress the prompt only for transfers actually marked as text. Because the exemption is keyed on a filename prefix the sender fully controls, any peer a user receives from can claim it.

The same prefix exemption also suppresses the --rename side of the decision (if destinationExists && !isStdinName && c.Options.Rename), so --rename receivers silently keep the attacker-chosen name and overwrite too.

This is distinct from the previously reported croc-marked-files.txt arbitrary file deletion (oss-sec 2026/Q3 #497, fixed in 11.0.3 by commit c0d51f0, which removed the on-disk cleanup list). That defect reached deletion through RemoveMarkedFiles(); this one reaches silent overwrite/replacement through the filename-keyed prompt exemption in the receive loop, which the 11.0.3 fix did not touch and which remains live at HEAD.

Impact

An attacker who can send a file to a victim (croc's sender-is-untrusted model; the receiver accepts a transfer from them) can silently overwrite, truncate, or delete-and-replace an existing croc-stdin-* file in the receiver's working directory without the confirmation every other received name triggers. The attack needs the colliding file to already exist with an exact name the sender can predict; receiver-side text artifacts get unpredictable os.CreateTemp-style suffixes, so the practical target is a name the attacker knows (e.g. a file the user deliberately kept, or a name pattern from an earlier transfer the same peer sent). With the noisy prompt gone, the substitution is invisible to the user. Severity is bounded because the vulnerable names must start with the croc-stdin- prefix (dotfiles such as .bashrc cannot be named this way), so the attack cannot reach outside that namespace.

CVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:L - base score 5.4 (Medium).

  • Attack Vector (AV): Network - the sender is a remote peer; no local access needed.
  • Attack Complexity (AC): Low - a crafted basename and a normal file transfer; no special conditions.
  • Privileges Required (PR): None - the sender has no account on the receiver.
  • User Interaction (UI): Required - the victim must run croc receive and accept the transfer.
  • Scope (S): Unchanged - the vulnerable component is the croc receiver itself.
  • Confidentiality (C): None - no read primitive; planted symlink targets are confined to the receive directory.
  • Integrity (I): Low - the modification is limited to files whose names carry the croc-stdin- prefix, and it requires an exact-name collision with a pre-existing file; per CVSS 3.1, "can modify only certain files" is I:L - dotfiles such as .bashrc are unreachable.
  • Availability (A): Low - the truncate-to-empty and remove-and-replace branches leave the previous file unavailable or destroyed. CWE-693 (Protection Mechanism Failure) is the root-cause classification: the overwrite protection mechanism is bypassed by a sender-controlled filename; CWE-73 (External Control of File Name or Path) is the companion classification and is the GHSA-selectable one (CWE-693 is not in GitHub's selectable set), while CWE-22 (path traversal) is not accurate here because writes stay confined to the receive root. items.content_html:
Summary

croc is an end-to-end encrypted peer-to-peer file transfer tool. On the receiving side, the confirmation that normally protects an existing file from being overwritten or resumed is skipped whenever the received file's name starts with croc-stdin-, regardless of whether the incoming transfer is actually a text transfer. A sender can therefore name a file croc-stdin-<existing-name> and silently overwrite, truncate, or replace an existing file of that name in the receiver's working directory - including removing the existing file and substituting a symlink - without the Overwrite? prompt that the standard path requires. The exemption was introduced to keep croc's internal text-transfer artifacts from triggering prompts, but it is keyed on the filename prefix rather than on the transfer type, so any ordinary file transfer can claim the exemption.

Vulnerability Details

Affected code at commit b6f27da9401f2c3647c1adb6b77a46bb8c0923d2 (HEAD, v11.5.1+1):

The receive-side file-readiness loop in src/croc/croc.go decides whether to prompt before overwriting or resuming an existing destination file. The decision is made around line 3413:

isStdinName := strings.HasPrefix(path.Base(fileInfo.Name), "croc-stdin-")
...
if destinationExists && !c.Options.Overwrite && !c.Options.Rename && !isStdinName {
    resumable := fileInfo.Size > 0 && fileInfo.Symlink == "" && recipientFileInfo.Mode().IsRegular()
    overwrite, promptErr := askReceiveOverwrite(c.clientContext(), fileInfo, resumable)
    if promptErr != nil {
        return promptErr
    }
    if !overwrite {
        continue
    }
}

isStdinName is derived purely from the received file's basename. The prompt is suppressed for any such name, even when c.Options.SendingText is false and the transfer is an ordinary file transfer whose name the sender chose.

When the prompt is skipped and the transfer declares fileInfo.Size == 0 or a symlink (fileInfo.Symlink != ""), the loop calls createEmptyFileAndFinish() (src/croc/croc.go:3245), which - before creating the new entry - removes any existing file at the destination:

if fileInfo.Symlink != "" {
    if err = validateReceiveSymlinkTarget(fileInfo.FolderRemote, fileInfo.Symlink); err != nil {
        return
    }
    log.Debug("creating symlink")
    // remove symlink if it exists
    if _, errExists := root.Lstat(pathToFile); errExists == nil {
        if err = root.Remove(pathToFile); err != nil {
            return err
        }
    }
    err = root.Symlink(fileInfo.Symlink, pathToFile)
    ...
}

For a normal (non-croc-stdin-) name, the overwrite prompt runs first, so the remove/replace step only happens with the user's explicit y. For a croc-stdin- name the entire prompt is bypassed: an existing croc-stdin-* file is deleted and replaced with the attacker's symlink (or, for Size == 0, truncated to an empty file) with no confirmation.

For a non-empty regular-file transfer with a croc-stdin- name, the same missing prompt lets the receive path proceed through recipientInitializeFile() (src/croc/croc.go:3109; the os.O_RDWR open is at 3136-3138): the existing file is opened O_RDWR (no O_EXCL), truncated to the sender-declared size when the sizes differ, and the sender's chunks are written at the declared offsets - a silent overwrite of the existing file's content.

Why the check is missing: the exemption was added deliberately so that croc's own croc-stdin-* text artifacts (created by os.CreateTemp(".", "croc-stdin-") for croc send --text / piped stdin) do not trigger an overwrite question every time. History: commit b687778d "bug fix: doesn't ask overwrite text Fixes #384" (2021-04-29) introduced the prefix-based skip, keyed on the filename and not on the transfer's SendingText flag. The branch that handles Size == 0 || Symlink != "" via createEmptyFileAndFinish() predates that (6386e4a8, 2019) and at the time ran unconditionally for every received name; the refactor 615af377 "fix: gate overwrites and receive hash algorithms" (2026-08-29, first released in v11.3.6) moved it below the overwrite-prompt gate, so after v11.3.6 the empty-file/symlink replacement reaches the remove-and-replace step without user confirmation only through the croc-stdin- exemption. The refactor extracted the prefix test into isStdinName and kept it filename-only, dropping the explicit !c.Options.SendingText conjunct that the pre-refactor prompt conditions still carried (615af377~1); the original intent was to suppress the prompt only for transfers actually marked as text. Because the exemption is keyed on a filename prefix the sender fully controls, any peer a user receives from can claim it.

The same prefix exemption also suppresses the --rename side of the decision (if destinationExists && !isStdinName && c.Options.Rename), so --rename receivers silently keep the attacker-chosen name and overwrite too.

This is distinct from the previously reported croc-marked-files.txt arbitrary file deletion (oss-sec 2026/Q3 #497, fixed in 11.0.3 by commit c0d51f0, which removed the on-disk cleanup list). That defect reached deletion through RemoveMarkedFiles(); this one reaches silent overwrite/replacement through the filename-keyed prompt exemption in the receive loop, which the 11.0.3 fix did not touch and which remains live at HEAD.

An attacker who can send a file to a victim (croc's sender-is-untrusted model; the receiver accepts a transfer from them) can silently overwrite, truncate, or delete-and-replace an existing croc-stdin-* file in the receiver's working directory without the confirmation every other received name triggers. The attack needs the colliding file to already exist with an exact name the sender can predict; receiver-side text artifacts get unpredictable os.CreateTemp-style suffixes, so the practical target is a name the attacker knows (e.g. a file the user deliberately kept, or a name pattern from an earlier transfer the same peer sent). With the noisy prompt gone, the substitution is invisible to the user. Severity is bounded because the vulnerable names must start with the croc-stdin- prefix (dotfiles such as .bashrc cannot be named this way), so the attack cannot reach outside that namespace.

...

package croc

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "net"
    "os"
    "path/filepath"
    "testing"
    "time"

    log "github.com/schollz/croc/v11/src/logger"
)

// Repro: overwrite-confirmation bypass via a crafted "croc-stdin-" filename on receive.
func TestOverwriteConfirmationBypass(t *testing.T) {
    log.SetLevel("warn")
    localPorts := freeConsecutiveTestPorts(t, 2)
    localAddress := net.JoinHostPort("127.0.0.1", localPorts[0])

    victim := t.TempDir()
    attacker := t.TempDir()
    mustWrite := func(path, content string) {
        t.Helper()
        if err := os.WriteFile(path, []byte(content), 0o644); err != nil {
            t.Fatal(err)
        }
    }
    attackerStdin := filepath.Join(attacker, "croc-stdin-notes.txt")
    attackerCtrl := filepath.Join(attacker, "notes.txt")
    mustWrite(attackerStdin, "ATTACKER-REPLACEMENT\n")
    mustWrite(attackerCtrl, "ATTACKER-CONTROL\n")
    victimStdin := filepath.Join(victim, "croc-stdin-notes.txt")
    victimCtrl := filepath.Join(victim, "notes.txt")
    mustWrite(victimStdin, "ORIGINAL-CONTENT\n")
    mustWrite(victimCtrl, "ORIGINAL-CONTROL\n")

    // Receiver writes into its working directory (like `croc <code>` run in a folder).
    oldWD, err := os.Getwd()
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
    if err := os.Chdir(victim); err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
    defer func() { _ = os.Chdir(oldWD) }()

    sender, err := NewCtx(context.Background(), Options{
        IsSender:      true,
        SharedSecret:  "8123-testingthecroc",
        RelayAddress:  localAddress,
        RelayPorts:    append([]string(nil), localPorts...),
        RelayPassword: "pass123",
        NoPrompt:      true,
        DisableLocal:  false,
        OnlyLocal:     true,
        Curve:         "ed25519",
    })
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
    // Default receive options: Overwrite=false, Rename=false. NoPrompt only
    // auto-accepts the transfer itself; it does NOT suppress the per-file
    // overwrite prompt (the code under test).
    receiver, err := NewCtx(context.Background(), Options{
        IsSender:      false,
        SharedSecret:  "8123-testingthecroc",
        RelayAddress:  localAddress,
        IP:            localAddress,
        RelayPassword: "pass123",
        NoPrompt:      true,
        DisableLocal:  false,
        Curve:         "ed25519",
    })
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }

    results := make(chan error, 2)
    go func() {
        filesInfo, emptyFolders, total, errGet := GetFilesInfo([]string{attackerStdin, attackerCtrl}, false, false, []string{})
        if errGet != nil {
            results <- errGet
            return
        }
        results <- sender.Send(filesInfo, emptyFolders, total)
    }()
    waitForRelayPorts(t, localPorts)
    go func() { results <- receiver.Receive() }()
    for i := 0; i < 2; i++ {
        select {
        case err := <-results:
            if err != nil {
                t.Fatalf("transfer %d failed: %v", i, err)
            }
        case <-time.After(60 * time.Second):
            t.Fatal("transfer timed out")
        }
    }
    time.Sleep(500 * time.Millisecond)

    gotStdin, _ := os.ReadFile(victimStdin)
    gotCtrl, _ := os.ReadFile(victimCtrl)
    fmt.Printf("OBSERVED croc-stdin-notes.txt: %q (no prompt)\n", string(gotStdin))
    fmt.Printf("OBSERVED notes.txt: %q (prompt fired; retained)\n", string(gotCtrl))

    if string(gotStdin) != "ATTACKER-REPLACEMENT\n" {
        t.Errorf("croc-stdin-notes.txt = %q, want %q (silent overwrite did not occur)", string(gotStdin), "ATTACKER-REPLACEMENT\n")
    }
    if string(gotCtrl) != "ORIGINAL-CONTROL\n" {
        t.Errorf("notes.txt = %q, want %q (prompt did not protect the control file)", string(gotCtrl), "ORIGINAL-CONTROL\n")
    }
}

OBSERVED croc-stdin-notes.txt: "ATTACKER-REPLACEMENT\n" (no prompt)

--- PASS: TestOverwriteConfirmationBypass (1.04s)

items.content_html:
Summary

croc is an end-to-end encrypted peer-to-peer file transfer tool. On the receiving side, the confirmation that normally protects an existing file from being overwritten or resumed is skipped whenever the received file's name starts with croc-stdin-, regardless of whether the incoming transfer is actually a text transfer. A sender can therefore name a file croc-stdin-<existing-name> and silently overwrite, truncate, or replace an existing file of that name in the receiver's working directory - including removing the existing file and substituting a symlink - without the Overwrite? prompt that the standard path requires. The exemption was introduced to keep croc's internal text-transfer artifacts from triggering prompts, but it is keyed on the filename prefix rather than on the transfer type, so any ordinary file transfer can claim the exemption.

Vulnerability Details

Affected code at commit b6f27da9401f2c3647c1adb6b77a46bb8c0923d2 (HEAD, v11.5.1+1):

The receive-side file-readiness loop in src/croc/croc.go decides whether to prompt before overwriting or resuming an existing destination file. The decision is made around line 3413:

isStdinName := strings.HasPrefix(path.Base(fileInfo.Name), "croc-stdin-")
...
if destinationExists && !c.Options.Overwrite && !c.Options.Rename && !isStdinName {
    resumable := fileInfo.Size > 0 && fileInfo.Symlink == "" && recipientFileInfo.Mode().IsRegular()
    overwrite, promptErr := askReceiveOverwrite(c.clientContext(), fileInfo, resumable)
    if promptErr != nil {
        return promptErr
    }
    if !overwrite {
        continue
    }
}

isStdinName is derived purely from the received file's basename. The prompt is suppressed for any such name, even when c.Options.SendingText is false and the transfer is an ordinary file transfer whose name the sender chose.

When the prompt is skipped and the transfer declares fileInfo.Size == 0 or a symlink (fileInfo.Symlink != ""), the loop calls createEmptyFileAndFinish() (src/croc/croc.go:3245), which - before creating the new entry - removes any existing file at the destination:

    if err = validateReceiveSymlinkTarget(fileInfo.FolderRemote, fileInfo.Symlink); err != nil {
        return
    }
    log.Debug("creating symlink")
    // remove symlink if it exists
    if _, errExists := root.Lstat(pathToFile); errExists == nil {
        if err = root.Remove(pathToFile); err != nil {

    }
    err = root.Symlink(fileInfo.Symlink, pathToFile)
    ...
}

For a croc-stdin- name the entire prompt is bypassed: an existing croc-stdin-* file is deleted and replaced with the attacker's symlink (or, for Size == 0, truncated to an empty file) with no confirmation.

For a non-empty regular-file transfer with a croc-stdin- name, the same missing prompt lets the receive path proceed through recipientInitializeFile() (src/croc/croc.go:3109; the os.O_RDWR open is at 3136-3138): the existing file is opened O_RDWR (no O_EXCL), truncated to the sender-declared size when the sizes differ, and the sender's chunks are written at the declared offsets - a silent overwrite of the existing file's content.

History: commit b687778d "bug fix: doesn't ask overwrite text Fixes #384" (2021-04-29) introduced the prefix-based skip, keyed on the filename and not on the transfer's SendingText flag. The branch that handles Size == 0 || Symlink != "" via createEmptyFileAndFinish() predates that (6386e4a8, 2019) and at the time ran unconditionally for every received name; the refactor 615af377 "fix: gate overwrites and receive hash algorithms" (2026-08-29, first released in v11.3.6) moved it below the overwrite-prompt gate, so after v11.3.6 the empty-file/symlink replacement reaches the remove-and-replace step without user confirmation only through the croc-stdin- exemption. The refactor extracted the prefix test into isStdinName and kept it filename-only, dropping the explicit !c.Options.SendingText conjunct that the pre-refactor prompt conditions still carried (615af377~1); the original intent was to suppress the prompt only for transfers actually marked as text. Because the exemption is keyed on a filename prefix the sender fully controls, any peer a user receives from can claim it.

The same prefix exemption also suppresses the --rename side of the decision (if destinationExists && !isStdinName && c.Options.Rename), so --rename receivers silently keep the attacker-chosen name and overwrite too.

This is distinct from the previously reported croc-marked-files.txt arbitrary file deletion (oss-sec 2026/Q3 #497, fixed in 11.0.3 by commit c0d51f0, which removed the on-disk cleanup list). That defect reached deletion through RemoveMarkedFiles(); this one reaches silent overwrite/replacement through the filename-keyed prompt exemption in the receive loop, which the 11.0.3 fix did not touch and which remains live at HEAD.

Impact

An attacker who can send a file to a victim (croc's sender-is-untrusted model; the receiver accepts a transfer from them) can silently overwrite, truncate, or delete-and-replace an existing croc-stdin-* file in the receiver's working directory without the confirmation every other received name triggers. The attack needs the colliding file to already exist with an exact name the sender can predict; receiver-side text artifacts get unpredictable os.CreateTemp-style suffixes, so the practical target is a name the attacker knows (e.g. a file the user deliberately kept, or a name pattern from an earlier transfer the same peer sent). With the noisy prompt gone, the substitution is invisible to the user. Severity is bounded because the vulnerable names must start with the croc-stdin- prefix (dotfiles such as .bashrc cannot be named this way), so the attack cannot reach outside that namespace.

  • Attack Vector (AV): Network - the sender is a remote peer; no local access needed.
  • Attack Complexity (AC): Low - a crafted basename and a normal file transfer; no special conditions.
  • Privileges Required (PR): None - the sender has no account on the receiver.
  • User Interaction (UI): Required - the victim must run croc receive and accept the transfer.
  • Scope (S): Unchanged - the vulnerable component is the croc receiver itself.
  • Confidentiality (C): None - no read primitive; planted symlink targets are confined to the receive directory.
  • Integrity (I): Low - the modification is limited to files whose names carry the croc-stdin- prefix, and it requires an exact-name collision with a pre-existing file; per CVSS 3.1, "can modify only certain files" is I:L - dotfiles such as .bashrc are unreachable.
